questions.question: State the approximate share of plastic in a modern car and explain, with reference to properties, why plastics replaced steel, glass and rubber in many parts.
questions.expected_answer: A modern car is about 10 per cent plastic by mass and 20 per cent or more by volume, roughly 100 to 150 kilograms in two hundred or more parts, compared with almost none in the 1950s. Plastics were chosen for lightness, since every kilogram saved reduces fuel use; formability, since a complex dashboard or bumper comes out of one mould in a minute in shapes steel cannot be pressed into; toughness, since a bumper bends and springs back; electrical insulation for wiring and connectors; corrosion resistance for tanks and liners that never rust; lower cost per part once the mould is paid for; and safety, since foam and soft trim cushion occupants. The body shell, chassis, engine and suspension remain steel because they carry the main loads and crash energy and run hot.

questions.question: Name the plastics used for a car's bumpers, lamp lenses, dashboard, fuel tank, under-bonnet parts and wiring, giving the reason for each.
questions.expected_answer: Bumpers are injection-moulded polypropylene with a honeycomb absorber, because it is light, tough and springs back from knocks. Lamp lenses are polycarbonate, because it is clear, light and shatterproof, with a hard coat against scratching and yellowing. The dashboard is a polypropylene or ABS skeleton with a PVC or polyurethane skin over polyurethane foam, giving shape, a good surface, sound deadening and cushioning. The fuel tank is blow-moulded multi-layer HDPE, which never rusts, is seamless, fits odd spaces and deforms rather than tears, with a barrier layer against vapour. Under the bonnet the air intake, engine covers and radiator end tanks are glass-filled nylon because it withstands heat and vibration. Wiring is insulated with PVC or cross-linked polyethylene and connectors are nylon, for electrical insulation and toughness.

questions.question: Discuss the effects of plastics on car safety and fuel use, and explain why end-of-life recycling of car plastics is difficult and what makers are doing about it.
questions.expected_answer: Plastics improved safety through padded dashboards, foam in doors and shatterproof lamp lenses, and lighter cars stop sooner; a 10 per cent reduction in mass saves about 5 to 7 per cent in fuel, lowering running costs and emissions, though plastics burn and must contain flame retardants. At end of life the steel and aluminium, about three quarters of the mass, are recovered by shredding and magnets, but the plastics are two hundred parts in a dozen polymer types, painted, glued, foamed and layered, so they cannot be sorted economically and most shredder residue goes to landfill; only large single-polymer parts such as bumpers and battery cases are easily recycled. Makers now mark each part with its polymer code, design parts to clip apart rather than glue, reduce the number of polymer types, and use recycled plastic in hidden parts such as wheel-arch liners.
